newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Animal lobby backs possible debt-for-ivory swap.
newsitem.headline: Animal lobby backs possible debt-for-ivory swap.

text.p: Two leading wildlife protection groups on Tuesday backed a proposal to write off debts of some African countries in exchange for existing ivory stocks.
But they strongly rejected a controversial proposal to end the world ban on the ivory trade.

Speaking on the sidelines of a Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) in Zimbabwe, officials from U.S.-based International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) and from Amsterdam-based Greenpeace, said they would also support other reasonable ways of handling a 100-tonne stockpile accumulated by three southern African states since the 1989 ban.
The proposal on ivory, and another proposal by Japan and Norway seeking to legalise whale-hunting, have become the dominant issues at the CITES conference.
"There should be no question of resuming trade. We are strongly opposed to that and we are recommending that CITES also reject this move," Barbara Maas of IFAW told a press briefing.
Elephant-rich Zimbabwe, Namibia, and Botswana are sponsoring a proposal at the 10-day CITES conference for a partial lifting of a ban on ivory sales.

The three countries and their supporters, notably Japan, say they must be allowed some limited but strictly supervised trade because their elephant population, now estimated at around 150,000, is increasing, and was doing so even before the ban seven years ago.

"Although we are saying the ban must stay, we are not opposed to other ways of handling existing stocks," Maas said, referring in particular to recommendations made by the African elephant countries after a meeting in Senegal earlier this year.

These included proposals that African ivory could be used in debt swaps or to establish an ivory bank reserve that could be traded 50 or so years later, once the world was sure trade would not endanger the African elephant.
Both Maas and Isabel McCrea of Greenpeace suggested that some Western countries could also compensate African states that burned their stocks.
Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe opened the CITES conference on Monday, calling for incentives for good wildlife management.

"There must be encouragement of sustainable utilisation and development for those whose policies and actions uphold scientifically accepted standards, while penalising those that abuse the environment," he said.
McCrea rejected arguments that African ivory trade would mainly benefit the poor. "The main beneficiary of trade is industry and it's no different wherever you are".
The proposal to allow ivory sales is strongly backed by Japan, which has promised to provide a market, and also by the 12-nation Southern African Development Community (SADC).

But it is stoutly opposed by many influential green movements and countries, including the U.S.-based African Elephant Foundation, and the United States and French governments. They argue lifting the ban will leave elephants at the mercy of poachers.
The 138-member CITES will vote on the issue and about 80 other proposals towards the end of the conference closing on June 20.

The other big issues on the CITES agenda include a proposal by Bolivia and the U.S. to list bigleaf mahogany, mainly found on the American continent, as an endangered species that must be traded under control.
